source.title: Large Language Models Relearn Removed Concepts
source.authors: M. Lo; Shay B. Cohen; Fazl Barez

record.tranche_reason: Measures how concept-related neuron activations are distributed in language models, extending the representation question to LLMs rather than testing the original toy-model geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper measures concept saliency across neurons and layers before and after pruning and retraining. Its NER performance results are not rows because they measure task recovery rather than the claim versions. The reported polysemanticity is measured after deliberate pruning and retraining, so it is not evidence that polysemanticity arises without that inducement. No SAE results or superposition geometry are tested.
record.test_reason: The study measures where a pruned NER concept's rank-based saliency reappears across layers after pruning and retraining. Its polysemanticity evidence is anecdotal top-activating tokens after deliberate pruning. None of this measures superposition geometry, capacity-driven sharing, spread of features across neurons in an unmodified model, SAE features, or feature dimensionality. It discusses polysemanticity without testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that pruned concepts move from later to earlier or middle layers, into neurons that previously encoded similar concepts. They conclude that relearned neurons become polysemantic, which makes permanent concept removal by pruning hard.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes LLMs for NER, identifies concept-related neurons with a probeless ranking, prunes neurons, retrains, and measures concept saliency and similarity. It does not use the original toy-model superposition method or measure overlapping directions.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report different redistribution patterns across architectures: DistilBERT and DistilGPT2 show increased saliency in middle layers, while GPT2 redistributes saliency approximately evenly. Random pruning also produces a different layer-wise pattern from concept pruning.

fits_no_version.finding: After the top-saliency half of neurons is pruned and the model retrained, location and person concepts reappear in remaining neurons, shifting toward middle layers (DistilBERT, DistilGPT2) or spreading evenly (GPT2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concepts removed by neuron pruning are relearned and relocated to remaining neurons within a few epochs of retraining.

fits_no_version.finding: Retrained neurons activate on both their original and the pruned concept (e.g. neuron 4148, Table 8; neuron 2405, Table 21), and their concept similarity to the original is mostly above 0.5 (Figs 6–10, Table 20). Evidence is anecdotal; the authors note large SDs (0.205, 0.199).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pruning-induced relearning makes neurons polysemantic, blending old and new concepts.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Only three model types and selected NER-related concepts are studied. The authors note that the relationship between concept similarity and saliency is not clear and report relatively large standard deviations for those measures. Layer-distribution values have no stated uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: NER performance-recovery results in Sections 6.1–6.2 and Appendix B were omitted because they do not measure the representation properties named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, overlapping directions or geometry.
Pruning half the neurons is followed by anecdotal polysemanticity, but capacity is never varied or controlled, and feature importance is never related to dedicated vs shared neurons.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measure of how many neurons a feature spreads over in an unmodified model (saliency is relative rank), and no dictionary or SAE recovery.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label is dropped. The saliency score is a normalized rank, so layer shares of salient neurons cannot speak to distributed or superposed representation. The polysemanticity reported is a product of deliberate pruning plus retraining, shown through a few top-activating-token examples. The study is better classed as model-editing/neuroplasticity work that mentions polysemanticity.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, overcomplete sparse features, overlapping directions, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular superposition geometry are tested.
The study does not test whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity, or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Polysemanticity is reported after intentional pruning and retraining; the study does not measure whether it arises without that inducement or establish it as evidence against superposition.
The study examines selected NER-related concepts and neuron activations in three models, not general feature decompositions or SAE recovery.
No SAE features or claims about their completeness, stability, or canonical status are tested.
The study does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: DistilBERT
rows.operation_detail: Measured the percentage of neurons per layer with concept saliency greater than 0.5 before pruning and after pruning the most salient half of neurons and retraining.

conditions.value: not stated for this layer-distribution result

rows.measure: Percentage of salient neurons by layer; values are base model → pruned and retrained
rows.note: The highest percentage shifts from layer 6 before pruning to layer 4 after pruning and retraining; salient neurons occur across multiple layers.
rows.check: Saliency is rank-based: neurons get scores by their 100-neuron group's position in a global ordering. So the share of neurons above 0.5 is fixed by construction, and its layer split cannot show whether a feature is spread across many neurons. The row measures concept relocation after pruning (neuroplasticity), not V4.

rows.subject: DistilGPT2
rows.operation_detail: Measured the percentage of neurons per layer with concept saliency greater than 0.5 before pruning and after pruning the most salient half of neurons and retraining.

conditions.value: not stated for this layer-distribution result

rows.measure: Percentage of salient neurons by layer; values are base model → pruned and retrained
rows.note: Salient neurons occur across multiple layers; layers 4 and 5 gain saliency while layer 6 decreases.
rows.check: Same rank-based saliency issue as R1; this is a layer-redistribution measure after pruning, not evidence on V4. Note that the text's §6.3 mislabels Table 7 as DistilGPT2; DistilGPT2 is in Table 6.

rows.subject: GPT2
rows.operation_detail: Measured the percentage of neurons per layer with concept saliency greater than 0.5 before pruning and after pruning the most salient half of neurons and retraining.

conditions.value: not stated for this layer-distribution result

rows.measure: Percentage of salient neurons by layer; values are base model → pruned and retrained
rows.note: The authors describe saliency as redistributing approximately evenly across the model after pruning and retraining.
rows.check: Same rank-based saliency issue as R1; it measures post-pruning redistribution in GPT2, not V4.

rows.subject: DistilGPT2
rows.operation_detail: Measured layer-wise percentage of neurons with concept saliency after randomly pruning the same number of neurons and retraining.

conditions.value: random; same number of neurons removed as in concept pruning

rows.measure: Percentage of salient neurons by layer; table lists base model → randomly pruned and retrained values
rows.note: The extracted table does not show layer labels alongside the values, so layer-to-value assignments are not made. The authors state that later layers gain salient neurons, while earlier and middle layers do not gain as many as under concept pruning.
rows.check: This is the random-pruning control for the same off-claim measure. Its 'base model' column (0.111, 15.481, …, 7.037) nearly matches Table 6's pruned-and-retrained column rather than its base column, so the baseline may be mislabeled. The layer order (presumably 0–6) is not printed.

rows.subject: DistilBERT
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean concept saliency by layer before pruning and after pruning and retraining.
rows.baseline: Base model: layers 5 and 6 have mean saliency 0.559 and 0.610, respectively; other layer values not stated
rows.value: After pruning and retraining: layers 3, 4, 5 and 6 have mean saliency 0.759, 0.797, 0.797 and 0.872, respectively
rows.note: The authors report that the concept becomes more evenly distributed over middle and later layers.
rows.check: Mean rank-based saliency by layer for person names after pruning; relocation measure, not V4. Only some layer values are given.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Location-name concepts in DistilBERT, DistilGPT2 and GPT2 after concept-neuron pruning and retraining; person-name concept in DistilBERT
reader_labels.reason: The measured concept saliency occurs across multiple layers and is redistributed across layers after retraining (R1, R2, R3, R5).
